The jury never hears him say a single word.
And all the while, beyond the walls, the paperwork of your own death keeps moving forward on a schedule, signed by people who will never once look you in the face.
On the sixteenth of April, 1999, Louisiana sets John Thompson's execution date, and marks it for the twentieth of May.
And in late April, 1999, he finds it — the crime lab report, the blood type, the proof on paper that had been sitting in the system the entire time.
This time the jury hears everything the first one never did.
His claim is simple and enormous: this office never trained its lawyers to follow the most basic rule of a fair trial, which is to turn over the evidence that helps the accused.
The decision lands on the twenty-ninth of March, 2011.
Justice Clarence Thomas writes for the majority, and his logic runs on a single rule that never blinks.
And a dissent frees no one and pays no one.
To win, Thompson had to prove not a single buried report but a pattern: that the office knew its lawyers would hide evidence and trained them anyway.
The Court said the office owed none of it.
A free man, told in the calm language of the law that eighteen years and fourteen death warrants had a price, and the price was zero.
He built a place in New Orleans for other exonerated men, people who, like him, had lost years, sometimes decades, to a mistake the State would never pay for.
He never saw a cent of his fourteen million.
The same voice a robbery conviction had once frightened into silence, the voice the jury in his murder trial was never allowed to hear.
